birmingham-city.intro: Small Heath roots, St Andrew’s and League Cup triumphs give Birmingham supporters plenty to put their knowledge to the test.
birmingham-city.history: Founded as Small Heath Alliance in 1875, Birmingham adopted the City name in 1943. St Andrew’s has been their home since 1906. The Blues reached the 1956 FA Cup final and won the League Cup in 1963 and 2011, while the Second City derby connects their story with Aston Villa.
birmingham-city.source_label: Birmingham City history and club profile

blackburn-rovers.intro: Ewood Park, early FA Cup successes and the 1994–95 Premier League title sit at the heart of Blackburn’s football story.
blackburn-rovers.history: Blackburn were formed in 1875 and became founding members of the Football League in 1888. Their honours stretch from five nineteenth-century FA Cups to the Premier League championship under Kenny Dalglish. Ewood Park has hosted Rovers since 1890, and Burnley provide the opposition in the East Lancashire derby.
blackburn-rovers.source_label: Blackburn Rovers history and club profile

bolton-wanderers.intro: Bolton’s story runs from Christ Church to the White Horse Final, with four FA Cup wins and a long Football League heritage.
bolton-wanderers.history: The club began as Christ Church in 1874 before taking the Wanderers name in 1877. Bolton helped found the Football League in 1888. Their 1923 FA Cup win came in Wembley’s first final, followed by further victories in 1926, 1929 and 1958. Later Premier League years brought European competition into the club’s story.
bolton-wanderers.source_label: Bolton Wanderers history and club profile

bristol-city.intro: Ashton Gate, a 1909 FA Cup final and a League One and Wembley trophy double make Bristol City’s history worth exploring.
bristol-city.history: Established in 1894, Bristol City entered the Football League in 1901 and won the Second Division in 1905–06. They finished second in the top flight the following season and reached the 1909 FA Cup final. In 2015, City combined the League One championship with their third Football League Trophy victory.
bristol-city.source_label: Bristol City history and club profile

burnley.intro: Claret and blue at Turf Moor connects Burnley’s identity with league championships, an FA Cup win and generations of Lancashire football.
burnley.history: Burnley were founded in 1882 and joined the original Football League in 1888. They became champions of England in 1920–21 and 1959–60, having won the FA Cup in 1914. Turf Moor has been their home since 1883, and the Clarets adopted their familiar claret and blue colours in 1910.

cardiff-city.intro: Cardiff’s 1927 FA Cup victory, blue-and-white identity and move from Ninian Park offer a distinctive Welsh football history.
cardiff-city.history: The club started as Riverside in 1899 and became Cardiff City in 1908. Their 1927 FA Cup win made them the only club from outside England to lift the trophy. After 99 years at Ninian Park, the Bluebirds moved to Cardiff City Stadium in 2009. Swansea are their South Wales derby rivals.
cardiff-city.source_label: Cardiff City history and club profile

charlton-athletic.intro: The Valley and the Addicks’ 1947 FA Cup win anchor a Charlton story that also includes years away from their familiar home.
charlton-athletic.history: Founded in 1905, Charlton joined the Football League in 1921. They followed their 1946 FA Cup final appearance by beating Burnley to win the competition in 1947. The Valley became their home in 1919, although ground problems later led to spells at Selhurst Park and Upton Park before their return.
charlton-athletic.source_label: Charlton Athletic history and club profile

derby-county.intro: Derby’s cricket-club origins, post-war FA Cup win and two 1970s league championships provide plenty of Rams history to explore.
derby-county.history: Derby County were formed in 1884 as an offshoot of Derbyshire County Cricket Club and helped establish the Football League four years later. They won the first post-war FA Cup in 1946. Their strongest league period came in the 1970s, with two First Division titles and a run to the European Cup semi-finals.
derby-county.source_label: Derby County history and club profile

lincoln-city.intro: The Lincoln Imp, red-and-white stripes and Sincil Bank give Lincoln City a local identity stretching back to the nineteenth century.
lincoln-city.history: Founded in 1884, Lincoln became original members of the Football League Second Division in 1892. Their Imps nickname comes from the city’s famous imp legend. They moved to Sincil Bank in 1895, while Graham Taylor’s 1975–76 Fourth Division championship remains a notable chapter in their league history.
lincoln-city.source_label: Lincoln City history and club profile

middlesbrough.intro: From Ayresome Park to the Riverside, Middlesbrough’s story includes recovery, a first major trophy and a European final.
middlesbrough.history: Boro were formed in 1876 and moved from Ayresome Park to the Riverside Stadium in 1995. After coming close to folding in 1986, they rebuilt and won successive promotions. Steve McClaren’s team delivered the League Cup in 2004 and reached the UEFA Cup final in 2006, adding two landmark occasions to the club’s history.

millwall.intro: Millwall’s journey from the Isle of Dogs to Bermondsey links the Lions’ identity with two Dens and an FA Cup final.
millwall.history: The club began as Millwall Rovers in 1885 and kept the Millwall name after leaving the area in 1910. They moved from the Old Den to the current Den in 1993. The lion on their crest supplies their nickname, and their 2004 FA Cup final appearance led to a first UEFA Cup campaign.

norwich-city.intro: Carrow Road, the Canaries’ yellow and green and a famous night in Munich make Norwich’s history instantly recognisable.
norwich-city.history: Norwich were founded in 1902 and have played at Carrow Road since 1935. League Cup wins in 1962 and 1985 preceded third place in the inaugural Premier League season. Their 1993–94 UEFA Cup campaign included victory at Bayern Munich, while their Canaries nickname reflects the area’s bird-breeding tradition.
norwich-city.source_label: Norwich City history and club profile

portsmouth.intro: Fratton Park and the Pompey name connect Portsmouth with FA Cup history and back-to-back championships of England.
portsmouth.history: Founded in 1898, Portsmouth joined the Football League in 1920. They won the FA Cup in 1939, then claimed successive First Division titles in 1948–49 and 1949–50. Their home is Fratton Park, and Pompey is a nickname shared with the city and its naval base. Blue shirts became part of their identity in 1912.

preston-north-end.intro: Deepdale and the original Invincibles place Preston North End at the centre of the Football League’s earliest history.
preston-north-end.history: Preston’s football club was officially founded in 1880, having developed from a cricket club. In 1888–89 they won the first Football League championship and the FA Cup without losing a match. That Double earned the Invincibles name. Deepdale and figures such as Tom Finney remain central to North End’s identity.
preston-north-end.source_label: Preston North End history and club profile

queens-park-rangers.intro: QPR’s West London story brings together Loftus Road, the 1967 League Cup and a near miss in the title race.
queens-park-rangers.history: The club traces its beginnings to Christchurch Rangers in 1882, taking the Queens Park Rangers name after a merger four years later. In 1966–67, Alec Stock’s side won both the Third Division championship and the League Cup. Rangers later finished just one point behind Liverpool in the 1975–76 First Division.
queens-park-rangers.source_label: Queens Park Rangers history and club profile

sheffield-united.intro: Bramall Lane, Sheffield’s cutlery heritage and four FA Cups help define the history of the Blades.
sheffield-united.history: Sheffield United were formed from the cricket club in 1889 and have played at Bramall Lane since their beginnings. The Blades nickname reflects the city’s cutlery industry. United won the league championship in 1897–98 and lifted the FA Cup in 1899, 1902, 1915 and 1925. Sheffield Wednesday are their Steel City derby rivals.
sheffield-united.source_label: Sheffield United history and club profile

southampton.intro: Southampton’s church-team origins link the Saints name with The Dell, St Mary’s and their memorable 1976 FA Cup win.
southampton.history: Founded in 1885, Southampton developed from a team associated with St Mary’s Church. They beat Manchester United to win the 1976 FA Cup while playing in the Second Division. After decades at The Dell, the club moved to St Mary’s Stadium in 2001. Their rivalry with Portsmouth is known as the South Coast derby.

stoke-city.intro: The Potters’ red-and-white stripes and journey from the Victoria Ground reflect Stoke-on-Trent’s football and industrial heritage.
stoke-city.history: Stoke were among the twelve clubs that founded the Football League in 1888. The City name arrived in 1925 after Stoke-on-Trent gained city status. Their Potters nickname comes from the local pottery industry. The club left the Victoria Ground in 1997 for the stadium now known as the bet365 Stadium.
stoke-city.source_label: Stoke City history and club profile

swansea-city.intro: Swansea’s rise from the Vetch Field to major silverware connects Welsh football traditions with a long place in the English leagues.
swansea-city.history: Founded as Swansea Town in 1912, the club became Swansea City in 1970. They left the Vetch Field for their current stadium in 2005. Three promotions in four seasons took them to the First Division in 1981; another rise brought Premier League football in 2011 and a League Cup victory in 2013.
swansea-city.source_label: Swansea City history and club profile

watford.intro: Vicarage Road and Graham Taylor’s climb through the divisions form the backdrop to Watford’s league and cup landmarks.
watford.history: Watford moved to Vicarage Road in 1922. During Graham Taylor’s first managerial spell, they rose from the fourth tier to the top flight and finished second in 1982–83. They reached the FA Cup final in 1984 and returned to that stage in 2019. Nearby Luton Town are their long-standing rivals.

west-bromwich-albion.intro: The Hawthorns, a throstle on the badge and generations of cup football give Albion a distinctive Black Country identity.
west-bromwich-albion.history: Formed in 1878, West Bromwich Albion became founding Football League members in 1888. They have played at The Hawthorns since 1900. Their honours include the 1919–20 league championship, five FA Cups and the 1966 League Cup. Navy-and-white stripes and the Black Country derby with Wolves are familiar parts of the Albion story.
west-bromwich-albion.source_label: West Bromwich Albion history and club profile

west-ham-united.intro: West Ham’s Thames Ironworks beginnings sit alongside Wembley triumphs, European honours and more than a century at the Boleyn Ground.
west-ham-united.history: The club began as Thames Ironworks in 1895 and took the West Ham United name in 1900. Their Boleyn Ground years lasted from 1904 until the move to London Stadium in 2016. Three FA Cups, the 1965 European Cup Winners’ Cup and the 2023 Conference League form key chapters in their honours history.
west-ham-united.source_label: West Ham United history and club profile

wolverhampton-wanderers.intro: Old gold at Molineux links Wolves with the Football League’s founders, Stan Cullis’s champions and the Black Country derby.
wolverhampton-wanderers.history: Wolves began as St Luke’s in 1877, took their present name in 1879 and joined the original Football League in 1888. Molineux has been their home since 1889. Under Stan Cullis they won the league in 1953–54, 1957–58 and 1958–59. Their best-known local rivalry is with West Bromwich Albion.
wolverhampton-wanderers.source_label: Wolverhampton Wanderers history and club profile

wrexham.intro: Wrexham’s Welsh Cup heritage and three successive promotions bring together one of Wales’s oldest football stories and its recent revival.
wrexham.history: Established in 1864, Wrexham have a long record in Welsh and cross-border football. Welsh Cup success brought European Cup Winners’ Cup campaigns, including a quarter-final in 1976. Winning the National League in 2022–23 began three promotions in successive seasons, carrying the club through League Two and League One to the Championship.

afc-wimbledon.intro: AFC Wimbledon’s supporter-led beginnings and climb from the ninth tier make their place at Plough Lane a story of rebuilding.
afc-wimbledon.history: Supporters established AFC Wimbledon in 2002 after the decision to allow Wimbledon FC’s relocation to Milton Keynes. The new club started in the Combined Counties League rather than inheriting a Football League place. Six promotions in thirteen seasons took them from the ninth tier to League One, with Plough Lane now their home.
afc-wimbledon.source_label: AFC Wimbledon history and club profile

barnsley.intro: Oakwell, the Tykes name and the 1912 FA Cup are the starting points for exploring Barnsley’s South Yorkshire football heritage.
barnsley.history: Reverend Tiverton Preedy founded Barnsley in 1887, and the club moved to Oakwell the following year. They joined the Football League in 1898. After losing the 1910 FA Cup final, they won the trophy against West Bromwich Albion in 1912. Their familiar red-and-white colours replaced blue in 1904.

blackpool.intro: Tangerine at Bloomfield Road brings Blackpool’s seaside identity together with the famous 1953 Matthews Final.
blackpool.history: Blackpool were founded in 1887 and moved to Bloomfield Road in 1901. Tangerine became their shirt colour in 1923. The club won the Second Division in 1929–30 and later enjoyed a strong period under Joe Smith. After FA Cup final defeats in 1948 and 1951, they lifted the trophy in 1953.

bradford-city.intro: Valley Parade and Bradford’s early FA Cup success provide the foundations for the Bantams’ West Yorkshire story.
bradford-city.history: Founded in 1903, Bradford City entered the Football League Second Division immediately. Their 1907–08 championship brought promotion to the top flight, and they won the FA Cup in 1911. Later promotions and relegations took the club through the divisions, with the 1984–85 Third Division title another notable achievement.
bradford-city.source_label: Bradford City history and club profile

bromley.intro: Hayes Lane and Bromley’s amateur cup heritage show how the club’s story stretches well beyond its recent league progress.
bromley.history: Bromley were formed in 1892 and helped establish both the Southern League and the London League. Their early honours included consecutive Isthmian League titles in 1908–09 and 1909–10. They won the FA Amateur Cup in 1911, 1938 and 1949, building a substantial non-League history before their modern professional league years.

burton-albion.intro: The Brewers name and the move from Eton Park reflect Burton Albion’s connection with the town’s brewing heritage.
burton-albion.history: Burton Albion were formed in 1950 and spent their early years in regional and non-League competitions. They moved from Eton Park to the Pirelli Stadium in 2005. Nigel Clough’s time as player-manager helped take the club through the Conference, culminating in the 2008–09 championship and entry into the Football League.
burton-albion.source_label: Burton Albion history and club profile

cambridge-united.intro: Abbey United’s beginnings and the U’s long association with the Abbey Stadium sit behind Cambridge United’s league journey.
cambridge-united.history: Founded as Abbey United in 1912, the club adopted the Cambridge United name in 1951. Their Abbey Stadium home dates to 1932. Successive Southern League championships in 1968–69 and 1969–70 helped them gain election to the Football League in 1970, before later promotions took them into the Second Division.
cambridge-united.source_label: Cambridge United history and club profile

doncaster-rovers.intro: Red-and-white hoops, Belle Vue and a return from non-League football are distinctive chapters in Doncaster Rovers’ history.
doncaster-rovers.history: Founded in 1879, Doncaster entered the Football League in 1901 and rejoined permanently in 1923 after earlier spells outside it. Their modern ground replaced Belle Vue in 2007. Rovers regained League status through the 2003 Conference play-offs, won the Football League Trophy in 2007 and reached the Championship through the 2008 play-offs.
doncaster-rovers.source_label: Doncaster Rovers history and club profile

huddersfield-town.intro: Huddersfield’s three successive league championships remain a landmark achievement in the history of the Terriers.
huddersfield-town.history: Founded in 1908, Huddersfield entered the Football League in 1910 and won the FA Cup in 1922. They then became champions of England in 1923–24, 1924–25 and 1925–26. Herbert Chapman led the first two title-winning seasons, with Cecil Potter completing the sequence. Those years remain central to the club’s football heritage.
huddersfield-town.source_label: Huddersfield Town history and club profile

leicester-city.intro: Leicester’s Fosse origins, Filbert Street years and collection of major honours give the Foxes a story across several eras.
leicester-city.history: The club began as Leicester Fosse in 1884 and became Leicester City in 1919, when the city received its official status. Filbert Street was their home from 1891 until the stadium move in 2002. Their honours include the Premier League, FA Cup and three League Cups, alongside two FA Community Shields.
leicester-city.source_label: Leicester City history and club profile

leyton-orient.intro: Brisbane Road and a history of changing club names make Orient’s East London identity an interesting one to explore.
leyton-orient.history: Leyton Orient’s roots go back to the Glyn Cricket Club in 1881, with football played under the Orient name from 1888. As Clapton Orient they joined the Football League in 1905. Promotion in 1961–62 brought a single top-flight season, and their later history included an FA Cup semi-final appearance in 1978.
leyton-orient.source_label: Leyton Orient history and club profile

luton-town.intro: Kenilworth Road and the Hatters’ 1988 League Cup win connect Luton’s familiar identity with major football occasions.
luton-town.history: Luton Town were founded in 1885 and have played at Kenilworth Road since 1905. Their first FA Cup final came in 1959. After winning the Second Division in 1981–82, they established a top-flight spell that included beating Arsenal 3–2 in the 1988 League Cup final.
luton-town.source_label: Luton Town history and club profile

mansfield-town.intro: Mansfield’s Wesleyan beginnings and rapid climb through the divisions in the 1970s offer a distinctive Stags history.
mansfield-town.history: The club began as Mansfield Wesleyans in 1897 and became Mansfield Town in 1910. They joined the Football League in 1931. Winning the Fourth Division in 1974–75 and the Third Division in 1976–77 took Mansfield to the Second Division for the first time, adding a notable promotion sequence to their record.
mansfield-town.source_label: Mansfield Town history and club profile

milton-keynes-dons.intro: Stadium MK, the 2007–08 double and a later Championship promotion are central chapters in the modern MK Dons story.
milton-keynes-dons.history: Milton Keynes Dons adopted their present identity in 2004 following Wimbledon FC’s relocation. They initially played at the National Hockey Stadium before moving to Stadium MK in 2007. The next season brought the League Two title and Football League Trophy. Karl Robinson’s side later won promotion to the Championship in 2015.
milton-keynes-dons.source_label: Milton Keynes Dons history and club profile

notts-county.intro: Meadow Lane and an 1862 founding date place Notts County among football’s most historically significant clubs.
notts-county.history: Notts County helped found the Football League in 1888 and won the FA Cup in 1894. Their long league history includes Tommy Lawton’s arrival in 1947 and Jimmy Sirrel’s promotions back to the First Division in 1981. The Magpies’ story also includes a more recent spell outside the Football League.
notts-county.source_label: Notts County history and club profile

oxford-united.intro: Headington roots, the Manor Ground and the 1986 League Cup win tell the story behind Oxford United’s football identity.
oxford-united.history: Oxford were founded as Headington in 1893 and took the Oxford United name in 1960. They entered the Football League in 1962 and reached the top flight through successive promotions in the 1980s. Their 1986 League Cup triumph remains a major landmark. The Kassam Stadium replaced the Manor Ground in 2001.
oxford-united.source_label: Oxford United history and club profile

peterborough-united.intro: London Road and a record-breaking first Football League season are part of what makes the Posh’s history distinctive.
peterborough-united.history: Peterborough United were formed in 1934 and won five consecutive Midland League titles from 1955 to 1959. Elected to the Football League in 1960, they immediately won the Fourth Division, scoring 134 league goals. Later play-off successes and promotions under Darren Ferguson added further second-tier chapters to their London Road story.
peterborough-united.source_label: Peterborough United history and club profile

plymouth-argyle.intro: Home Park, green shirts and the Mayflower on the badge connect Plymouth Argyle directly with the city’s maritime history.
plymouth-argyle.history: Argyle were founded in 1886 and have played at Home Park since 1901. The Pilgrims nickname recalls the group that left Plymouth for the New World in 1620, with the Mayflower represented on the crest. Green and white have been the club’s predominant colours throughout much of its history.
plymouth-argyle.source_label: Plymouth Argyle history and club profile

reading.intro: The Royals’ Berkshire identity and their earlier Biscuitmen nickname offer two different ways into Reading’s football story.
reading.history: Reading were established in 1871 but did not join the Football League until 1920. Their first top-flight season came in 2006–07. The Royals name reflects Berkshire’s royal association, while Biscuitmen recalled Huntley & Palmers. A 1988 Full Members’ Cup win and FA Cup semi-finals in 1927 and 2015 feature among their cup landmarks.

sheffield-wednesday.intro: The Wednesday cricket-club connection and a long list of honours give the Owls a history rooted in Sheffield.
sheffield-wednesday.history: The football club was formed in 1867 from The Wednesday Cricket Club and retained the Wednesday Football Club name until 1929. They were the Football Alliance’s first champions before joining the Football League. Four league titles, three FA Cups and a League Cup form part of their record, with Hillsborough their home.
sheffield-wednesday.source_label: Sheffield Wednesday history and club profile

stevenage.intro: The Boro’s journey from regional football to the League includes a delayed promotion and a successful second attempt.
stevenage.history: Stevenage were founded in 1976 and reached the Conference in 1994. They won it in 1995–96 but were denied Football League promotion because of ground standards. Winning the Conference again in 2009–10 finally secured entry. The Borough name was shortened to Stevenage, and a play-off promotion followed in their first League season.

stockport-county.intro: Edgeley Park and the Hatters name link Stockport County’s football identity with the town’s industrial past.
stockport-county.history: Founded as Heaton Norris Rovers in 1883, the club became Stockport County in 1890. Edgeley Park has been their home since 1902, and the Hatters nickname recalls local hat-making. Their 1990s successes included second-tier football and a League Cup semi-final in 1996–97, alongside several Wembley appearances.
stockport-county.source_label: Stockport County history and club profile

wigan-athletic.intro: Springfield Park, a late Football League election and a move to a new stadium mark stages in Wigan’s football journey.
wigan-athletic.history: Wigan Athletic were formed in 1932 and built their early record in the Cheshire County League, Lancashire Combination and Northern Premier League. They were elected to the Football League in 1978. A first promotion followed in 1981–82, and the club left Springfield Park for its present stadium in 1999.
wigan-athletic.source_label: Wigan Athletic history and club profile

wycombe-wanderers.intro: Adams Park and Martin O’Neill’s successful non-League years provide the backdrop to Wycombe’s progress through the divisions.
wycombe-wanderers.history: Wycombe were founded in 1887 and spent much of their history in the Isthmian League. Under Martin O’Neill they won the FA Trophy in 1991 and 1993 and the Conference title in 1992–93. Their Football League years later included FA Cup and League Cup semi-final runs in 2001 and 2007.
wycombe-wanderers.source_label: Wycombe Wanderers history and club profile

accrington-stanley.intro: Accrington Stanley’s modern story starts with a rebuilt club, the Crown Ground and a name made famous beyond football.
accrington-stanley.history: The present Accrington Stanley was formed in 1968 after the earlier club’s collapse. That predecessor, founded in 1891, had played in the Football League from 1921 to 1962. Stanley’s home is the Crown Ground. A 1989 milk advert brought national recognition to the name, but the club’s football roots are much deeper.
accrington-stanley.source_label: Accrington Stanley history and club profile

barnet.intro: From Underhill to The Hive, Barnet’s Bees identity brings together North London football and a long non-League heritage.
barnet.history: Barnet’s history traces back to 1888 in Chipping Barnet. Underhill was their home from 1907 until the move to The Hive in 2013. The modern club’s development also included the 1912 merger of Barnet Avenue and Alston Works. A long Athenian League spell brought seven championships and an FA Amateur Cup victory.

bristol-rovers.intro: Rovers’ route through Eastville, Bath and the Memorial Stadium reflects a club history shaped by several different homes.
bristol-rovers.history: Bristol Rovers were founded in 1883 and reached the Football League in 1920 after Southern League success. Their 1952–53 Third Division South title brought second-tier football. After leaving Eastville, they spent ten years at Twerton Park in Bath before returning to Bristol at the Memorial Stadium in 1996.
bristol-rovers.source_label: Bristol Rovers history and club profile

cheltenham-town.intro: Whaddon Road and Cheltenham’s late-1990s breakthrough connect the Robins’ long non-League years with Football League success.
cheltenham-town.history: Cheltenham Town were formed in 1887 and spent decades in local and Southern League football. Under Steve Cotterill they won the FA Trophy in 1998 and the Conference championship in 1998–99. Those achievements brought first-time Football League membership, followed by promotion through the 2002 Third Division play-offs.
cheltenham-town.source_label: Cheltenham Town history and club profile

chesterfield.intro: The town’s Crooked Spire, Saltergate and two club record-holders give Chesterfield’s Spireites identity its own landmarks.
chesterfield.history: Chesterfield’s nickname refers to the town’s famous Crooked Spire. The club left Saltergate for its present stadium in 2010. Dave Blakey made 617 league appearances, while Ernie Moss scored 162 league goals. These figures and the changes of home ground provide distinctive threads through the club’s history.

colchester-united.intro: Colchester’s famous 1971 FA Cup victory and a rise to the Championship add memorable moments to the U’s history.
colchester-united.history: Founded in 1937, Colchester United entered the Football League in 1950. Their 3–2 FA Cup win over Don Revie’s Leeds United in 1971 remains a standout result. After a brief Conference spell, they returned as champions in 1992. Promotion in 2006 brought Championship football and a tenth-place finish the following season.
colchester-united.source_label: Colchester United history and club profile

crawley-town.intro: Crawley’s progression from Sussex leagues to professional football gives the Red Devils a history of gradual growth and major breakthroughs.
crawley-town.history: Crawley’s roots date to 1896, with the Town name adopted in 1958. They moved through local leagues before entering the Southern League and eventually won its Premier Division in 2003–04. Becoming fully professional in 2005 preceded a difficult financial period, but Steve Evans later led them to the Conference title in 2010–11.
crawley-town.source_label: Crawley Town history and club profile

crewe-alexandra.intro: Gresty Road and the Railwaymen nickname connect Crewe Alexandra’s football story with the Cheshire town’s railway heritage.
crewe-alexandra.history: Crewe were formed in 1877 as the football section of a cricket club named after Princess Alexandra. They reached the FA Cup semi-finals in 1888 and helped found the Football League Second Division in 1892. Their long stay in the lower divisions later changed under Dario Gradi, who began his managerial tenure in 1983.
crewe-alexandra.source_label: Crewe Alexandra history and club profile

exeter-city.intro: St James Park, supporter ownership and a remarkable 1914 South American tour give Exeter City a distinctive football identity.
exeter-city.history: Exeter’s roots date to St Sidwell’s United in 1901. The club moved to St James Park in 1903 and adopted the Exeter City name in 1904. The Grecians are owned through their supporters’ trust. Their 1914 South American tour included the first match against a Brazil national team, before Football League entry in 1920.

fleetwood-town.intro: Highbury Stadium and the Cod Army name connect Fleetwood’s football identity with the Lancashire coast and several club rebuilds.
fleetwood-town.history: Fleetwood’s original club was formed in 1908, while the current incarnation was established in 1997. Earlier versions competed in the Lancashire Combination and Northern Premier League before financial difficulties led to changes. Highbury Stadium is their home, and supporters use the Cod Army name alongside the traditional Fishermen nickname.
fleetwood-town.source_label: Fleetwood Town history and club profile

gillingham.intro: New Brompton origins, Priestfield and two fourth-tier championships provide the foundations for exploring the Gills’ Kent football history.
gillingham.history: Gillingham were founded as New Brompton in 1893 and took their current name in 1912. They entered the Football League in 1920, lost membership in 1938 and returned in 1950. League championships in 1963–64 and 2012–13 are notable honours, while the 2000–2005 period brought their first sustained second-tier spell.

grimsby-town.intro: Blundell Park and the Mariners nickname reflect Grimsby’s coastal identity, while Alan Buckley’s teams added major Wembley memories.
grimsby-town.history: Founded as Grimsby Pelham in 1878, the club adopted the Town name a year later and moved to Blundell Park in 1898. They reached two FA Cup semi-finals in the 1930s. Under Alan Buckley, Grimsby won both the Football League Trophy and a promotion play-off at Wembley in 1998.
grimsby-town.source_label: Grimsby Town history and club profile

newport-county.intro: Newport’s European cup adventure and the Exiles’ rebuilding years are distinctive chapters in the club’s South Wales story.
newport-county.history: The club was formed in 1912 and joined the Football League’s new Third Division in 1920. A Welsh Cup win in 1980 led to the European Cup Winners’ Cup quarter-finals the following year. After the club folded in 1989, it was reformed; difficulties returning to its old ground helped establish the Exiles nickname.
newport-county.source_label: Newport County history and club profile

northampton-town.intro: Northampton’s rapid climb to the First Division in the 1960s remains one of the most striking passages in the club’s history.
northampton-town.history: Founded in 1897, Northampton entered the Football League in 1920 after success in the Southern League. Under Dave Bowen, three promotions in five years carried them from the Fourth Division to the First. Their top-flight stay lasted one season, ending in 1966, before subsequent relegations returned them to the fourth tier.
northampton-town.source_label: Northampton Town history and club profile

oldham-athletic.intro: Boundary Park and Joe Royle’s successful years connect Oldham’s Pine Villa origins with Wembley and Premier League football.
oldham-athletic.history: Oldham began as Pine Villa in 1895 and adopted the Athletic name after moving to Boundary Park in 1899. Their Football League entry came in 1907. Joe Royle later led them to the 1990 League Cup final and the 1990–91 Second Division title, bringing top-flight football and a place in the inaugural Premier League.
oldham-athletic.source_label: Oldham Athletic history and club profile

port-vale.intro: Vale Park, Burslem and Roy Sproson’s extraordinary appearance record provide a distinctive route into Port Vale’s Potteries history.
port-vale.history: Port Vale helped found the Football League Second Division in 1892. After earlier homes in Cobridge and Hanley, they returned to Burslem when Vale Park opened in 1950. Roy Sproson played 842 competitive matches for the club and is commemorated outside the ground. Matches with Stoke City are known as the Potteries derby.
port-vale.source_label: Port Vale history and club profile

rochdale.intro: Spotland and the Dale nickname anchor Rochdale’s history, which includes an unusual early League Cup final appearance.
rochdale.history: Rochdale were formed in 1907 and joined the Football League when the Third Division North was created in 1921. Spotland has been their home since 1920. They reached the League Cup final in 1962 and later spent a lengthy period in the fourth tier, with Bury and Oldham among their established rivals.

rotherham-united.intro: The Millers’ merger origins and move from Millmoor to New York Stadium connect several eras of Rotherham football.
rotherham-united.history: Rotherham United were created in 1925 by merging Rotherham County and Rotherham Town. They won the Third Division North in 1950–51 and reached the inaugural League Cup final in 1961. After leaving Millmoor and a temporary spell at Don Valley Stadium, they moved into New York Stadium in 2012.
rotherham-united.source_label: Rotherham United history and club profile

salford-city.intro: Salford’s journey from local amateur football to national attention began long before the familiar modern Ammies story.
salford-city.history: The club was founded as Salford Central in 1940 and later competed in the Manchester League. Regional cup successes marked the 1970s before the Salford City name was adopted in 1989. Former Manchester United players and Peter Lim acquired the club in 2014, adding a new chapter to its Moor Lane history.
salford-city.source_label: Salford City history and club profile

shrewsbury-town.intro: Shrewsbury’s regional league beginnings and return through the Conference play-offs provide plenty of Salop history to explore.
shrewsbury-town.history: Founded in 1886, Shrewsbury built their early record in local and Midland competitions before entering the Football League in 1950. They won the Third Division in 1978–79. After falling into non-League football in 2003, they returned immediately through the 2004 play-offs, while 2018 brought both EFL Trophy and League One play-off finals.
shrewsbury-town.source_label: Shrewsbury Town history and club profile

swindon-town.intro: The County Ground, Don Rogers and a Wembley win over Arsenal make Swindon’s League Cup story a memorable one.
swindon-town.history: Swindon’s roots date to 1879, and the club settled on the Town name in 1883. They entered the Football League in 1920 after Southern League success. In 1969 they beat Arsenal 3–1 to win the League Cup, with Don Rogers a key figure in a season that also brought promotion.
swindon-town.source_label: Swindon Town history and club profile

tranmere-rovers.intro: Prenton Park and John King’s promotion-winning teams frame Tranmere’s journey from Belmont beginnings to Wembley success.
tranmere-rovers.history: The club was founded as Belmont in 1884 and became Tranmere Rovers the following year. Prenton Park has been their home since 1912. John King’s second managerial spell brought promotion in 1989, the Associate Members’ Cup in 1990 and a further promotion through the play-offs in 1991.
tranmere-rovers.source_label: Tranmere Rovers history and club profile

walsall.intro: The Saddlers nickname and the move from Fellows Park reflect Walsall’s links with local industry and its football past.
walsall.history: Walsall were formed in 1888 by combining Walsall Town and Walsall Swifts. They helped found the Football League Second Division in 1892. The Saddlers name recalls the town’s saddle-making heritage. After almost a century at Fellows Park, the club moved to Bescot Stadium in 1990.

york-city.intro: York’s Minstermen identity, an FA Cup semi-final and a Wembley double offer distinctive moments for supporters to revisit.
york-city.history: The present York City club was founded in 1922 and joined the Football League seven years later. Their best FA Cup run reached the semi-finals against Newcastle United in 1954–55. In 2012 they won the FA Trophy and secured a return to the Football League in the same season. Their home is York Community Stadium.
york-city.source_label: York City history and club profile
